title: TA9-22703
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: These are the reasons I reject the refugee claims of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, a 33 year old citizen of Colombia. In addition, I reject the related claims of her 41 year old husband, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, her 20 year old step-son, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, her 3 sons; 14 year old, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, 11 year old, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX Camacho, and 1 and a half year old XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, all citizens of Colombia.

The claimant alleges a personal lap top computer and other electronic equipment was stolen from the family apartment in XXXXX 2009. The computer contained sensitive personal XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

In early XXXXX 2009, she received demands from Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) by telephone to provide the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and be prepared to assist the FARC in gaining access to XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. When the calls and threats continued she made a report to the police on XXXXX, 2009. On the advice of the police she changed both her cell and land line telephone numbers.

On XXXXX, the claimant again received a telephone call from the FARC on the new cell phone number indicating that because of her actions as an informer, she, her husband and step-son, were now considered military targets.
On XXXXX, the claimant's believe there was an attempt to take her son from school. It was only because of the action of the school in phoning the father, that this attempt was unsuccessful.
The claimants fled Colombia together in XXXXX 2009 and after a short stay in the United States of America (USA), they came to Canada and made refugee claims.

There are unresolved credibility concerns that affect the core elements of the claim. In addition, I am satisfied the claimants did not establish that for them, on a balance of probabilities, state protection would be inadequate. Hence I reject the claims for refugee protection. ANALYSIS Credibility Did the claimant receive phone calls from FARC in 2009?

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, she did not. In her oral and written evidence, she indicated the calls started in XXXXX 2009. Further in oral evidence she stated her problems with the FARC started in XXXXX 2009. The police report, (Exhibit C-11) made XXXXX, 2009, shows the initial date of Commission of the threats as XXXXX, 2009. The claimant suggested this could have been an error in translation. In the hearing room, the interpreter looked at the original Spanish report and verified the initial date as XXXXX, 2009, as indicated at page 18 of the disclosure, Exhibit C-11.
I am satisfied that the claimant making a report at the end of XXXXX 2009 of phone calls beginning in early XXXXX, would not report to the police the calls started XXXXX.

Due to the inconsistencies, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant did not receive threatening phone calls as she outlined in her Personal Information Form, Exhibit C-1, narrative. As a result, I make a negative credibility inference. Did the claimant store personal XXXXX information on a lap top computer stolen in XXXXX 2009?

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, she did not. The police report from XXXXX 2009, Exhibit C-10, shows a number of pieces of electronic equipment were stolen from the claimant's apartment; there is no mention that the laptop computer contained sensitive, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant explained that when she made the XXXXX 2009 report she only told the police what was stolen. I find this to be implausible, that a XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX would not report to the police that there was sensitive information on her stolen computer. Further, I believe she would have reported the theft immediately to her employers as well as the police and not have waited until six weeks after the threatening calls began, to speak with someone within the company. Furthermore, it is simply implausible that a major XXXXX XXXXX would even allow an employee to download onto a personal computer XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

I find this entire account of having XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX stolen and not reporting the nature of the theft to the police and her employer, not credible. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that this account has been created to support her refugee claim.

There is no independent evidence to support there was an attempt to kidnap the claimant's son, that she changed her cell phone number or that she received phone calls from persons suspected to be members of the FARC. Her employment letter makes no mention of her problems with the FARC.

Since I am satisfied that the claimant did not possess XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX and did not receive phone calls from the FARC in 2009 as claimed on this basis, her claim, and the related claims fail.

In the alternative, even if the account was accepted as credible, which clearly is not the case; did the claimant establish that for her and her family, state protection would be inadequate? I am satisfied they did not.
My analysis consists of two parts.
Part I is a review of the documentary evidence to establish that in XXXXX, Colombia is making serious efforts to provide adequate protection for its citizens who fear FARC.
Part II is an analysis of the claimant's evidence provided to establish that these efforts would on a balance of probabilities provide inadequate protection.

The current United States Department of State Report for 2009, found in Exhibit R-1, item 2.1, states: * Recent elections were generally considered fair and free * The internal conflict continued between the government and terrorist organizations * Civilian authorities generally maintained control of security forces with some exceptions * The government has made efforts to confront human rights abuses * FARC and ELN committed human rights abuses including: * Political killings * Use of landmines * Killing of duty members of security forces * Kidnappings * Forced displacements * Intimidation of judges, prosecutors and witnesses * Recruitment of child soldiers * Attacks against human rights activists. * Killing of teacher and trade unionists * New illegal armed groups are targets of security force action but lack the organization, search and military capacity of the former AUC Page 2 * Kidnappings decreased by 18 percent * Mass killings decreased by 13 percent * During 2008 the Ministry of Defense relieved from duty, 80 officers and 213 NCO and soldiers for unethical conduct.1 * Human Rights Unit obtained convictions against 421 defendants * 87 members of Congress and other politicians were linked to paramilitary groups, some were convicted * Paramilitary and new illegal groups operate in areas without a strong government presence Page 5 * The new judicial system has resulted in a conviction rate of 60% as opposed to the old conviction rate of 3% Page 8 * The Prosecutor General's Office operated 13 satellite offices specializing in investigating human rights crimes. * The Inspector General's Office investigates misconduct by public employees Page 10 * Government forces continued to use civilian informants Page 12 * The government has initiated reforms to improve the human right performance of the security forces including new rules of engagement * The Ministry of Defense reported 2,481 members of guerrilla groups demobilized * Indigenous persons demobilized from the 34th and 6th fronts of FARC Page 13 * The 8000 to 9,000 member FARC and 2000 member of ELN work together in many areas attacking government forces and demobilized paramilitary while in other areas they fight each other * The FARC is reported as killing persons suspected as collaborating with government authorities (the only specific reference to XXXXX is the terrorist attack on a Blockbuster outlet in January 2009) * The Majority of kidnappings were reported as a result of common crimes * FARC and ELN were reported as responsible for a total of 49 cases of kidnapping * Military action freed 81 kidnap victims * FARC and ELN established check points on rural highways * Enhanced government security presence on major highways is reported as reducing the number of kidnappings

This review of the United States, Department of State, Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 2009 satisfies me that Colombia is a functioning democracy where civilians have recourse to security forces when they require protection from criminal acts and human rights investigators for protection from human rights abuse. Those accused of such acts are held accountable for their actions through the rule of law.
Historically, Colombians have feared left wing guerrillas, the FARC, the National Liberation Army (ELN) and right wing paramilitary groups such as the United Self Defense Forces of Colombia (AUC).

Many Colombian governments in the past took steps to control the FARC and ELN with marginal success. Since 2002, the current government, with the assistance of the US, has committed significant resources to protecting its citizens from harm, from the two left wing groups.

Of particular interest in reviewing the current situation as it pertains to FARC in Colombia today, are the two reports by the International Crisis Group 4.1 from April 2008 and 4.5 from March 2009. Both are recent and all statements are fully documented. In addition, the Group is guided by well known and respected international personalities, including a former Prime Minister of Canada and an internationally recognized Canadian jurist.

The first report outlines the problems that the current Uribe government has created for FARC since 2002. * Many experienced commanders have been killed by security forces, assassinated by other insurgents, or died. This has severely disrupted communications and internal cohesion. * No Colombian political party any longer supports FARC as a legitimate left-wing force. * FARC's command structure after six years of sustained military pressure is believed to be faltering due to a lack of internal communication. * Security forces believe FARC is less operational, i.e. in 2007 there were only between 9,000 to11,000 fighters supporting FARC as opposed to approximately 19,000 in 2002, and only 10 of its former 71 fronts are currently regularly active. * The new government policy is to expand the presence of security forces in remote areas to re-establish the rule of law in these areas. * FARC units now have specialized in the use of land mines and attacks against specific police and military targets. * FARC is managing to infltrate armed force commands. * To compensate for losses, rural fronts are being reinforced with urban militia. * FARC is attemtping to regain legitimacy in the rual population by avoiding harm to civilians while focusing on high impact military targets.

The more recent 2009 report notes: * Key units of FARC have withdrawn to the jungle and mountains. * New tactics rely on ambushes. * At the tactical level, structures have decentralized; however, the Secretariat is capable of co-ordinating actions around the country. * Even though FARC has replaced its leaders in its senior command, co-ordination between senior and mid-ranking commanders is difficult. * Demobilized fighters remain in big cities to decrease the risk of being targeted by FARC. * After pushing FARC out of heavily populated areas and regaining control of road arteries, ..., the secuity forces are focusing on attacking traditional FARC strongholds. * Areas where FARC is strong and active are noted - western Meta, Purumayo, high mountain ranges or tropical jungle. (None of these include large urban populations.) * Security forces fear FARC will attempt to win back status in urbans areas through terrorism. Police have seized caches of explosives in the outskirts and FARC commandos have been arrested when attempting to penetrate cities. The first two complete paragraph of page 12 indicate FARC urban structures have been disrupted; however, insurgents remain active in Cali and Bueneventura. Now FARC work in independent cells, support networks have been progressivly weakened. In the early 2000's, urban fronts were driven out of cities like Bogota, Medellin, Cali and Cucuta. Security forces have made logistics vulnerable to interception and exert tight control via checkpoints on roads and rivers that lead from combat areas. * Extortion may have increased but is under-reported. Individuals may be using FARC's name as a mean to extract extortion. * Drug revenues have dropped from one billion to 500-600 million per year. * ELN leadership has called for an alliance with FARC; however, this generally has not occurred. In areas where ELN formations have been decimated, there have been links with FARC fronts. * Section 8 (page 15) states that in urban areas FARC support has vanished. Tens of thousands marched in XXXXX against FARC in March 2008. FARC continues to control remote areas. * FARC is actively working with youth in universities to again create a base of political support. * Security forces have increased to more than 400,000 in 2007 and have been successful in forcing FARC to retreat. Since 2007, security forces have expanded their presence in rural areas. * The insurgents are not close to defeat for a number of reasons; however, the government strategy aimed at a military victory is showing visible results as of 2007.

The theme of the International Crisis Group reports is reflected in the research of the Board. Item 4.3 of Exhibit R/A-12 at page 3 indicates that a news report in February 2008 reported FARC is relying on drug trafficking for its financial support since kidnapping and extortion are in decline.
In addition, the Colombian Minister of Defense indicated to the BBC that FARC currently lacks means of communication.
I reviewed the balance of the evidence found in Exhibit R-1, specifically as it pertains to FARC's ability to track and personally harm a person of interest in XXXXX.

Item 2.2, is the Human Rights Watch Colombian Report for 2009. This report indicates FARC murdered a human rights defender in Meta in October 2009 and were responsible for a massacre of 17 Awa in Narino. There is no report of FARC being responsible for similar acts in XXXXX.

Item 2.4, is the report by Amnesty International (AI) Colombia 2009. AI reports that indications of kidnappings and hostage taking showed improvements but other areas deteriorated, such as, internal displacement, threats against human rights defenders and killing of trade unionist. The FARC is identified as responsible for bomb attacks in urban areas. I would note that such actions would be more of the nature of terrorist attacks not personally directed at a particular individual. When the report indicates specific incidents, none are identified as occurring in XXXXX.

In December the government provided victims of abuses by paramilitary or guerrilla groups compensation. Of the 437 kidnappings in 2008, criminal gangs were thought to be responsible for the majority. Where kidnappings were conflict related, guerillas were responsible.
Item 2.5, is the United Nations Human Rights Council report for 2008. It acknowledges the government's efforts to strengthen the rule of law.

FARC and the ELN are criticized for recruitment of children, violence against women, the use of land mines and the holding of hostages. At page 10, the report speaks specifically as to the actions of the FARC, in the murder of four coca leaf eradicators in Cordoba and an army informer in Bolivar. There is no mention of any such action in XXXXX.

Acts of terrorism from 2008 are reported in paragraph 29. None of these were in XXXXX, however, I acknowledge in other more recent documents there are attacks of terrorism reported in XXXXX in 2009. Specifically, kidnappings are reported in paragraph 39 but again, none from XXXXX. Paragraph 75 and 76 outlines groups at risk, including, human rights defenders and trade unionist. Paragraph 79 mentions the government's efforts to protect human rights workers.
Item 4.3, COL102779, quotes a number of sources that as of February 2007, FARC no longer operates in the departments of Cundinamarca and Bogoca.

Item 4.4, COL102787, quotes a United Nations representative as stating, that children are not forcibly recruited but volunteer to join FARC. Amnesty International states that other information indicates forcible recruitment does occur.
Item 7.3 COL201407, from 2007 reports kidnappings ...took place in rural areas.

Item 10.1, is the September 2009 CSIS report concerning Colombia's efforts to counter the guerrilla's threats. In the summary page (V11 and V111) it notes the basis of the Uribe Administration's plan. The efforts to develop an improved military including greater use of helicopters, is outlined. The report states that the improved armed forces and better tactical execution since 2002 have pushed insurgents away from cities and towns. The FARC still controls territory and can launch small-scale operations. This has been emphasized since when I read all the evidence, both that entered by the Board and by various counsels, this is a repeated theme.

Details of the government's efforts are provided in the balance of the report. Colombia's efforts to control corruption are noted at page 44 where the international indicators show a rise from 25 in 1998 to 50 in 2008. Further Colombia now ranks as fifth best in Latin America, in a Corruption Perception Index for 2008.

Item 14.7 is a recent RIR COL103286, the research department of the Board was unable to find written reports that would indicate FARC or the ELN did track victims who move within Colombia. A Human Rights Watch researcher, supported by a professor from Acadia University, stated their belief that FARC would have the capacity to continue to target a person of interest. Similarly, a professor from Stetson University stated the two groups are capable if the person's threat or interest warrants such effort. A Colombia professor, at the National University, stated his opinion that it is likely impossible to track a victim who relocates from one area to another.

The report continues to show the difference in opinion among academics when it discusses the risk to persons returning from abroad. The professors from Acadia University here in Canada and from Stetson University in the United States, both are of the opinion that regardless of the passage of time, FARC could track a person if they had sufficient interest. Neither provided any supporting evidence that in recent years, FARC or ELN used this capacity to track a person(s) into XXXXX or other urban areas and harm that person(s) after finding him or her.

The professor from the Colombia University is of the opinion that the efforts of the government forces have made it unlikely that a person relocating could be found and harmed. The opinion is shared in a report published by the Foundation for Security and Democracy in December 2008.

Even with conflicting views among academics, the review satisfies me that the State of Colombia is making serious efforts to provide adequate protection for its citizens who fear the FARC. These efforts are not always perfect but are most successful in urban areas such as XXXXX. Part II

The Federal Court of Appeal has stated in Carrillo3 that the burden of proof now shifts to the claimant to establish with probative, reliable and relevant evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, these efforts by the state will result in at best, inadequate protection for them.

Prior to the XXXXX, 2009 police report, the claimant was not harmed physically nor was she confronted face to face by members of FARC. When she reported the calls to the authorities, XXXXX, 2009, she was told to change her phone numbers and that the police would do an investigation. The claimant never returned to the police to provide the additional information that another unwanted phone call had been received or that an attempt to abduct her child had been made. I note that the attempt to abduct the child was made in person and that an independent witness, the school official, would have been able to provide some details of the attempted abduction to the police.

The fact, the claimant made no follow-up with the police, even after the police had indicated a willingness to investigate, does not establish protection would be inadequate, but only that the claimant did not make serious efforts to access protection.

Counsel referred to the newest UNHCR guidelines for refugees from Colombia, Exhibit C-15. These guidelines identify eleven groups whose profile puts them at added risk of persecution. However the claimant and his family are not from any of the 11 identified profiles of those reported as being most at risk in Colombia in this report.

Counsel's news reports, Exhibit C-14 does not give an account of persons similarly situated to the claimants i.e., person from XXXXX who refused to follow FARC directions being harmed in XXXXX. At page 31, of Exhibit C-14, a reporter for the Miami Herald indicates in a section titled, Trouble Spots, does not indicate XXXXX is such a spot.

My reading of these reports and many similar reports connected to other claims; satisfies me that FARC is still a viable force of approximately 10,000 with headquarters in the south of Colombia. When the FARC operates outside its areas of control they do so in the nature of terrorist's attacks and are often captured as indicated in counsel's disclosure at page 49 and 50 of Exhibit C-14. In these attacks outside their controlled areas, FARC is looking for media attention. Victims tend to be security forces or those identified by UNHCR in its report, Exhibit C-15.

Since the claimant did not follow up with the security forces after XXXXX, 2009, the claimants are not of the profile of those identified by UNHCR as being most at risk and the claimants were unable to show reliable evidence that persons similarly situated to them, have suffered serious harm in XXXXX recently, I am satisfied the claimants have not established with reliable probative and relative evidence, that for them, state protection would be inadequate, should they return to XXXXX where they have lived in the past.
The claimant's account of her problems with the FARC was not credible.

The claimants have failed to establish there is a serious possibility they will be persecuted or suffer other forms of serious harm should they return to XXXXX, Colombia, where they lived in the past.

Hence, the Refugee Protection Division rejects the claims pursuant to both section 96 and section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
